prompt: Write a ~700-word piece of literary short fiction about: a child's map of a city that does not exist yet. Prose only, no headings.
text:
The paper was stiff and smelled faintly of citrus and new ink, the kind of sharp scent that usually meant something important was coming to stay in the corner of Leo's room where it belonged with his other treasures: a dried leaf from last autumn, a smooth river stone he'd found behind his grandmother's house, and a bottle cap painted gold. But this wasn't just any map; it was a blueprint for a city that had not been born yet. The ink lines were drawn in pencil first, then reinforced with black marker where the streets felt most certain to him, while other areas remained hazy sketches of blue rivers winding through grey blocks, waiting for permission to exist on watercolor paper he hadn't even bought.

To anyone else looking at it from across the room, the drawing would have seemed chaotic and nonsensical. There were no grid lines aligning perfectly with any compass rose; instead, the roads curved organically, dictated by Leo's intuition of how a creature made up entirely of stories should flow. He had started in the center, marking a massive square where he decided the city's heart would beat—a place for festivals and fountains that never froze over. From there, branches of asphalt radiated outward not toward logic or zoning laws, but toward whimsy and necessity alike. One street zigzagged violently up a hill because Leo insisted it led to a library built inside a hollowed-out mountain; another snaked lazily along the bottom edge where he placed shops that sold things people didn't know they wanted until they saw them: clouds in jars, whispering windchimes, and ice cream made from moonlight.

He spent hours every evening at his small wooden desk, refining the edges of this impossible place with a precision that belied its fantastical nature. He would tilt his head sideways to judge whether the bridge spanning the ink-blue river looked sturdy enough for giant turtles or if it needed more arches to support dreams carrying travelers across without them ever tiring. Sometimes he paused, staring at the blank white space between two plotted districts and filled in a park before remembering there wasn't one yet, adding a cluster of trees with leaves drawn as tiny spirals that turned slowly clockwise whenever someone told a joke nearby.

The city had no name on it, not because Leo hadn't thought of many possibilities—Aetheria, Somnambula, The City of Unwritten Names—but because he knew the true title would change depending on who was walking its streets and what season they were in. It existed only in this folded packet within his backpack, a secret parallel universe that operated entirely outside the reach of satellites or cartographers with rulers and protractors. In Leo's world, gravity worked differently; houses floated slightly off their foundations to catch drafts singing lullabies, and rain fell upwards on Tuesdays so puddles could fill themselves naturally without umbrellas opening against them.

His mother once asked what he was drawing when she walked in unexpectedly while the lights were dimmed by sunset. "A place," Leo had said softly, not stopping his hand as he shaded a fountain with grey ink that shimmered like oil on water. "Somewhere people can go if they are lost." She hadn't pressed for details about architecture or population density; she simply nodded and asked if it was true that the bakery there made bread that tasted exactly like childhood memories of home, even when you were far away from where those homes stood.

As he worked late into the night, surrounded by shadows that seemed to stretch toward his drawings rather than recede, Leo realized this map wasn't about escaping reality but about mapping a potentiality that could only be touched through belief. Every line was an invitation for someone else to believe too, and every filled-in square was proof that even before construction began or first footsteps tread the ground, we are all architects of where tomorrow might begin. The city would never appear on any official gazetteer; it would remain a private geography known only by those who knew how to read between the strokes of graphite and ink, finding their own way home in a place that didn't yet exist but was already waiting for them with open doors made of starlight and cobblestones paved over secrets.
topic: a child's map of a city that does not exist yet
